component.name: GitBraid
component.summary: Read your Git history as coloured lanes

description.p: GitBraid is a desktop Git client that draws history as coloured lanes, so the shape of a branch is visible before you read a word of it.
Made for people who want to see what git is doing, not be shielded from it:

ul.li: Several repositories open at once in tabs, each keeping its own history, selection and commit draft
Stage, unstage and discard by file or by individual hunk
A full-width diff viewer with side-by-side view, syntax colouring and whitespace-only changes hidden on request
Conflicts handled in the app: a banner while a merge or rebase is suspended, per-file resolution, and Abort or Continue
Merge commits show what they brought in, what the other side had, and what a person resolved by hand
Branch, remote and tag operations from context menus that explain why an entry cannot run
Git-Flow built on plain git, writing the same config keys the command line tool uses
An activity log of every git command the app ran, with how long each took

description.p: GitBraid carries no runtime dependencies and shells out to the real git, so nothing it does is invisible to the command line.

description.p: Every action now has an output window that fills while git is still talking, and says whether it is still going or how it ended. Failures always open it; switching branches never does.

Naming a repository on the command line now opens it — gitbraid followed by a path, or a folder handed over by a file manager. The desktop file had been promising that since the first release and nothing read the argument. A second one raises the window already open and adds a tab.
There is a Flatpak manifest, built and run rather than merely written. It builds git into the sandbox, because the runtime does not ship it and every operation here is a git command.

A stash is one row in the history instead of three, drawn so it reads as set-aside work rather than as a commit, and every stash is shown rather than only the newest. Right-clicking one offers the commands that apply to a stash.
The sidebar has the search box every other list already had, for branches, tags, remotes and stashes.
Four keyboard shortcuts were firing on any modifier combination ending in the same letter, so Ctrl+Shift+P pushed the branch and Ctrl+F fetched every remote. They no longer do.
The engine underneath is twelve Chromium releases newer, bringing security fixes GitBraid had been going without, and the renderer now runs sandboxed.
The diff pane scrolls on a layer of its own, so it no longer repaints the change map beside it. Twelve thousand rows scroll at 11.6 ms a frame where they took 22.9.

GitBraid opens without keeping you waiting. Launching from the dock left a loading cursor spinning for about ten seconds, and no icon beside it, over a window that had been on screen since the second.

Pressing a tab selects it. A press that moved more than a few pixels was read as the start of a drag, and the click that would have chosen the tab went with it — so on a touchpad the tab often did not change at all.

Clicking a tab works from anywhere. With file history, release notes, preferences or the repository manager open over the window, the switch happened but nothing on screen changed — the panel was still covering it, still showing the repository you had left.
Files can be picked in groups and acted on together: staged, discarded, stashed or saved as a patch, with every menu entry naming how many it will touch.
Any file can be ignored — adapting to whether git already tracks it — or followed back through its history in a panel of its own, renames included, carrying the whole diff viewer.
Tabs can be dragged into the order you want. A finished update asks before restarting rather than taking the window, and a half-written commit message now survives a restart.
Large diffs draw only the rows on screen, in every view: unified, side-by-side and wrapped. A twelve-thousand-line diff went from about nine frames a second to a steady seven milliseconds a frame.
A failed git command now opens a dialog with the line that explains it and the whole of git's output, and Git-Flow refuses a version number that is already tagged before it changes anything.
Side-by-side keeps its halves even and its divider in the middle, the diff has a horizontal scrollbar that is always in reach, and the change map doubles as the pane's scrollbar.

Small repairs. Letters with tails are no longer clipped in text boxes, dialogs stop marking branch names and URLs as misspelt, and the commit panel shows an author's photograph rather than only initials.

The change map keeps quiet when the whole diff is already on screen, Check for Updates has moved into the Help menu, and the buttons in Repository management carry icons and match each other's height.
GitBraid can now fetch and install its own updates, checking each download against the checksum published with the release and refusing anything it cannot verify.

Author pictures come from GitHub when the commit address is one GitHub issued, and an address with no picture anywhere keeps a disc of initials rather than a pattern invented from it. Commit search has a field of its own, the diff shows a map of where its changes are, and finishing a git-flow branch asks the remote whether the branch is really there instead of trusting a stale tracking ref.

Large histories stay smooth: only the commit rows on screen are drawn, so scrolling holds a steady frame whether the history is four hundred commits or nine thousand, and switching tabs no longer re-reads it.

Nothing changes the repository behind your back either. Clicking a branch moves the view to it; checking out takes a double-click, and warns first when there is uncommitted work. Merging asks which way round it goes before it runs, and finishing a git-flow branch can now publish the result and clear the branch off the remote.
GitBraid no longer asks gravatar.com for author photos unless you turn them on. Nothing leaves the machine by default.
Five fixes: two places that claimed something which had not happened, two that held memory they no longer needed, and a guard on discarding changes.
First working build.
